messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# James Chen's Reckoning

James Chen was fifty-two years old when the bomb went off at the civic center in Portland, a building he had entered dozens of times as a journalist covering city council meetings and local politics. He had been standing in the lobby, waiting for a source, when the explosion tore through the east wing. The blast threw him backward against the marble floor. What he remembers most vividly—what plays in his mind with unbearable clarity even now, twenty-one years later—is the taste of copper and ash in his mouth as he lay there, ears ringing, unable to move. He remembers the smell of burnt concrete mixing with something chemical and wrong. Seventeen people died. He survived with a fractured collarbone and lacerations across his left side. He was one of the lucky ones. Everyone told him so.

For the first few months after the bombing, James returned to work. He filed stories, attended press conferences, interviewed survivors. He appeared functional. But around the eighteen-month mark, after his divorce from Margaret had been finalized—she had grown tired of his distance, his irritability, his refusal to go anywhere public—he began to notice that certain things had started to unravel. A photograph of the bombed building, printed in an archive he was researching, sent him into a panic so acute he had to leave the newsroom. The image triggered an immediate spike in his vigilance; he found himself listening for unusual sounds in his apartment for hours afterward, scanning for threats that weren't there. To manage the anxiety that followed, he had impulsively purchased an expensive leather chair that he positioned so his back was always against the wall, allowing him to see the entire room at once. The purchase felt necessary, almost urgent, a way to regain control after the photograph had shattered his sense of safety.

James had come to believe that if he allowed himself to truly think about what happened—to sit with the memory rather than push it away—he would lose his grip entirely. The memory itself felt unreal to him, a film so extreme that his mind sometimes rejected it as something that could have actually occurred. Yet when the memory did break through, it felt like the bombing was happening again in real time: the pressure of the blast, the copper taste flooding his mouth, the helplessness. This conviction that thinking about the event would destroy him made him acutely sensitive to anything that might trigger the memory. When a colleague mentioned an unpredictable schedule change, James felt his threat system ignite; unpredictability itself had become dangerous because it meant he could not prepare, could not anticipate, could not keep the memory at bay. He responded by spending three thousand dollars on a security system he barely used, then another two thousand on a vacation he cancelled. The spending was compulsive, a way to distract himself from the thought that he was spiraling, that he would never feel normal again.

The more James tried not to think about the event, the more the memory replayed. When he sat in restaurants, he found himself noticing potential weapons—a steak knife, a heavy glass, the proximity of exits—and his body would go rigid, seized by a freezing response that made it impossible to continue eating or speaking. His colleagues had stopped inviting him to lunch. The threat monitoring had become constant: he listened obsessively for sounds that might mean someone was entering his apartment, even though he lived on the fourth floor of a secure building. He could not relax, even when he was objectively safe. The hypervigilance fed the conviction that something terrible was coming, that he had lost the capacity to feel genuine emotion, that nothing held meaning anymore. A specific taste—something acrid and metallic that sometimes appeared in his morning coffee—would catapult him back into the memory, and the memory would confirm his worst fear: that he was trapped in a cycle he could not escape.

At seventy-three, James has finally come to therapy. His retirement is approaching, and the thought of having nothing but time to sit with his own mind terrifies him. What he fears most is that the memory will consume him entirely, that the feelings he has been outrunning for two decades will finally catch up. What he hopes for, though he barely dares to articulate it, is that he might feel something genuine again—not happiness necessarily, but the possibility that his life could mean something beyond the moment the world exploded.

violation_explanations: Triggers (photograph, colleague's schedule change, taste in coffee) appear throughout, but no paragraph explicitly conveys that triggers directly drive or lead to maladaptive strategies; instead, maladaptive strategies (chair purchase, security system, compulsive spending) are described as responses to anxiety and threat, not directly to triggers themselves.

Negative appraisals (belief that thinking about the event will destroy him, conviction that he has lost capacity for genuine emotion, fear of being trapped in a cycle) appear, but no paragraph shows these beliefs directly driving maladaptive strategies; the strategies are framed as responses to threat and memory instead.
Memory appears vividly throughout, but no paragraph conveys that the memory itself triggers or activates the triggers (photograph, taste, sounds); rather, external stimuli trigger the memory.

Maladaptive strategies (chair purchase, security system, compulsive spending, avoidance) are described, but no paragraph shows these strategies producing or reinforcing negative appraisals; the causal direction is not established.
Maladaptive strategies are described, but no paragraph conveys that these strategies activate or produce triggers; the relationship is absent from the narrative.
